details:
**Black Forest source (Brigach and Breg at Donaueschingen)**
The Danube rises in Germany's Black Forest, where the Brigach and Breg streams join at the town of Donaueschingen. It is Europe's second-longest river after the Volga, about 2,850 km (1,770 miles) long. It flows through or along ten countries, and the ancient Greeks and Romans called its lower course the Ister.

**Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade**
The Danube flows through four national capitals, more than any other river in the world: Vienna (Austria), Bratislava (Slovakia), Budapest (Hungary) and Belgrade (Serbia). In Belgrade it meets the Sava beside Great War Island. Other cities on its banks include Ulm, Ingolstadt (where the Illuminati were founded in 1776), Passau, Linz, Novi Sad (capital of Serbia's Vojvodina province) and Galați in Romania.

**Iron Gates (Đerdap)**
A long gorge where the Danube cuts between the Southern Carpathians and the Balkan Mountains, forming the border between Serbia and Romania. The 19th-century Sip Canal was built to help ships pass its rapids, but it was later flooded by Đerdap Lake, the reservoir of the Iron Gate hydroelectric dams completed in 1972.

**Ada Kaleh**
A Danube island that was a Turkish (Ottoman) exclave with a mosque and fortress. It was submerged in the early 1970s when the Iron Gate I dam raised the river level. Some of its buildings were meant to be moved to the nearby island of Șimian.

**Budapest: Buda and Pest**
The Danube divides hilly Buda on the west bank from flat Pest on the east; the two were united in 1873 to form Hungary's capital. Landmarks include the Széchenyi Chain Bridge, Margaret Island with its Art Nouveau water tower, and Heroes' Square, whose monument honors the seven chieftains of the Magyar tribes.

**Vienna: Kunsthistorisches Museum and Schönbrunn Palace**
Austria's capital on the Danube is home to the Kunsthistorisches Museum, which holds the world's largest collection of paintings by Pieter Bruegel the Elder, and to the Habsburg summer residence of Schönbrunn Palace. A branch of the river, the Danube Canal, runs along the historic Innere Stadt (Inner City).

**Tisza, Sava, Drava and other tributaries**
Major tributaries include the Tisza (its longest, joining in Serbia), the Sava (its largest by flow, joining at Belgrade), the Drava (from Croatia), the Morava, the Inn, and the Siret and Prut in Romania. The Siret joins near Galați.

**"Iller, Lech, Isar, Inn" mnemonic**
A German schoolchildren's rhyme lists the Bavarian tributaries. The Iller, Lech, Isar and Inn flow in from the right (south), and the Altmühl, Wörnitz, Naab and Regen from the left (north).

**Danube Delta and the Black Sea**
The Danube empties into the Black Sea through a large delta, mostly in Romania with part in Ukraine, just north of the Razim–Sinoe lagoons. The delta is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and Ramsar wetland, and Ukraine's dredging of the Bystroe Channel through it caused controversy. An international commission of member states works on protecting the river basin.

**Main–Danube Canal**
A canal completed in 1992 that links the Danube to the Main River, a tributary of the Rhine. It creates a continuous waterway across Europe from the North Sea to the Black Sea.

**Trajan's Bridge and the Tabula Traiana**
Roman emperor Trajan's architect Apollodorus of Damascus built a bridge over the lower Danube around 105 CE for the campaign against Dacia. For over a thousand years it was the longest arch bridge ever built. The Tabula Traiana, a Roman memorial plaque, was raised to higher ground when the Iron Gate dam flooded the gorge. Nearby, a huge rock carving of the Dacian king Decebalus overlooks the river.

**Huchen (Danube salmon)**
A very large salmonid fish found only in the Danube basin. It is endangered, and hatchery-raised fry have been released to restore wild populations.

**"The Blue Danube"**
The famous 1866 waltz by Johann Strauss II, titled "An der schönen blauen Donau." Questions often joke that the river is nowhere near as blue as the waltz suggests.

**Lepenski Vir**
A Mesolithic and early Neolithic archaeological site on the Serbian bank in the Iron Gates region. It is known for sandstone sculptures with fish-like human faces. It was moved to higher ground when the dam reservoir flooded its original location.

**Pollution disasters**
In 2000, cyanide from a gold mine at Baia Mare, Romania, spilled into the Someș River and from there into the Tisza and the Danube. In 2010, red sludge from an alumina plant near Ajka, Hungary, reached the Danube. Industrial waste pools also line the river at Almásfüzitő.
